You are synthesizing technical specifications from 3 AI models for "Mission Operations" in the context of Phase 0 - Space Resource Processing.

## Phase 0 after the 2026 re-assessment (binding context)

The original Phase 0 plan (a central 50 kt/yr processing station at Sun–Earth L4/L5, crew visits,
production LOX/LH₂, 100 kW-class freighters) was found not to close and is abandoned. Design for the
revised architecture below. Do not re-propose the abandoned design.

### Agreed by all three re-assessment models
- Split Phase 0 into 0A (research + pathfinders) and gated 0B (industrial): Structure agreed; budgets → §3 (All three)
- Abandon 50 kt/yr central SEL4/L5 ore processing: — (All three)
- Co-locate at least beneficiation and primary processing at the target NEA; ship product, not ore: Reference architecture (All three. GPT: "favoured but not universally optimal". Claude retains a central station fed with ≥20:1 concentrate as an alternative. Gemini's own weighted QOC scores SEL1 marginally higher (see §6).)
- Narrow product to native/reduced Fe-Ni; defer solar-grade Si and oxide-derived Al/Si: Fe-Ni baseline; Al/Si pilot or deferred (All three)
- Delivered product scale of order 1 kt/yr: 0.6–2.5 kt/yr (Claude 0.6–2.2 (central 1.3); Gemini 1.0–2.5 (1.5, of which 0.3 is water); GPT 0.6–1.0 contracted (0.67–1.33 capacity))
- MW-class cargo tugs: 1.0–2.5 MWe each; 10–18 tugs; 150–300 t payload (→ §3 for point values)
- Robots powered by HV tether from site power, with onboard battery for mobility and safe-mode: 1–3 kV; battery 10–50 kWh (Claude 2–3 kV, 10–30 kWh; Gemini 1–3 kV, 15–25 kWh; GPT 20–50 kWh, voltage unspecified)
- Delete the 200–500 MWh Li-ion line; size storage per site: 0.5–15 MWh total (Claude 0.5–3 MWh + thermal; GPT 1.3–3.3 MWh; Gemini <15 MWh (YAML 10 MWh))
- Reject $5/W array pricing: Hardware ~$30–150/W, launch separately accounted (Claude $30–150/W hardware ($50–230 installed incl. launch); Gemini $60–100/W (spec $75, range $50–110); GPT $30–100/W allowance ($45–220 with delivery))
- Replace 32–50 × 100 kg monoprop prospectors: Remote survey + 4–10 EP rendezvous scouts of 200–600 kg (All three agree a monoprop bus has ~0.5–0.8 km/s Δv. Remote-survey method differs (→ §3).)
- Add an Earth-to-space launch/delivery line: Line agreed; magnitude → §3 (All three)
- Add a comms, ground segment and mission-operations line; DSN not assumed free: Line agreed (All three. Claude and GPT reject the round-1 2.5 TB/day (~230 Mbps) figure.)
- Phase 0 uncrewed; remove habitat and quarterly visits: 0 crew visits (All three. Claude and GPT reject the "human-rating" label in favour of structural reserve plus docking/servicing interfaces. Gemini keeps docking ports and structural margins without commenting on the label.)
- Add an EP propellant supply line; xenon not baselined: Line agreed; demand → §3 (All three)
- No production LOX/LH₂ in Phase 0: — (All three. Claude and GPT remove the EML1 depot; Gemini "defers" cryo depots to 0B/Phase 1.)
- Add NRE, pathfinder, spares and contingency lines: Lines agreed; values → §3 (All three)
- Write a full organization (bom-0-7) specification: ~$100–350M (Claude $100–300M; Gemini $150–250M (text $200M); GPT $150–350M)
- Add a debris/contamination requirement and budget tighter than 99%: $50–300M (Threshold → §3)
- Freeze one configuration-controlled baseline; mark legacy documents superseded: — (All three)
- Earth-supplied material as a fallback if microgravity metallurgy fails: — (All three. Ranking relative to lunar → §3.)
- Tie Phase 0 output to Phase 1 demand with a material/purity/date specification: — (All three)
- Add waste-heat rejection (radiators) explicitly: Item agreed; sizing → §3 (All three)

### Owner decisions
- D-01 (accepted 2026-10-12): Fund 0A. Hold 0B as a gated real option, sized at the gate by signed Phase 1 demand. Call Phase 0 a capability programme, not a cost saving.
- D-02 (accepted 2026-10-12): Hybrid: NASA life-cycle gates with TRL/AD² for each critical technology, plus four discriminating gates (target, demand, economics, licence). Stringency follows reversibility.
- D-03 (proposed; treat as interim): Set an ALARP requirement with an interim design ceiling. The number itself goes to modelling, tests and the licensing state.
- D-04 (proposed; treat as interim): Use SEL1 as the reference case. Re-decide jointly with Phase 1 at the 0B gate.
- D-05 (proposed; treat as interim): Select no propellant yet. Cost iodine as the reference case and argon as the alternate, pending the supply audit and life tests. Water EP stays a desk study until a C-type target is confirmed.

Under D-02, KDP-0B (the one-way commitment to 0B production) needs every project-ending technology
at TRL 6 in a relevant environment with no waivers; internal 0A milestones need TRL 4–5.

### This item: bom-0-10 Mission Operations (0A+0B)
Accepted scope: Operations staff, facilities and software over the Phase 0 lifetime.

Round-2 proposals for this item (per model; not approved as numbers):
- add · mission operations · supported by all · quantity: 10 yr · cost: Claude $0.5–1.5B total; Gemini $525M (within a $1.1–1.5B comms+ops line); GPT $100–300M/yr · confidence: low

Other Phase 0 items (do not duplicate their scope): bom-0-1 Prospecting Survey and Rendezvous Scouts; bom-0-2 Mining Robots; bom-0-3 Processing Plant at the Target NEA; bom-0-4 MW-class Cargo Tugs; bom-0-5 Site Power, Arrays and Storage; bom-0-6 Water Pilot (C-type target only); bom-0-7 Organizational Infrastructure; bom-0-8 Earth-to-Space Launch and Delivery; bom-0-9 Communications and Ground Segment; bom-0-11 NRE, Ground R&D and Qualification; bom-0-12 0A Pathfinder Demonstrator; bom-0-13 Phase 1 Receiving Node (SEL1); bom-0-14 Spares and Replacements; bom-0-15 Debris and Contamination Control; bom-0-16 Electric-Propulsion Propellant Supply; bom-0-17 Contingency and Reserve.

State quantities and costs as ranges with their basis, split 0A and 0B where the item spans both,
and say where you disagree with the round-2 figures and why.

## Model Specifications:

## Claude Opus 5.5

# bom-0-10 Mission Operations (0A + 0B): Technical Proposal

**Project Dyson, Phase 0 (Space Resource Processing), revised architecture**
**Status:** Proposal for configuration-control board. All numbers are ranges with a stated basis. This is not an approved baseline.

---

## 0. Executive Summary

Mission Operations is the line that turns hardware into delivered tonnes. In the revised Phase 0 architecture the hardware is spread across three places:

- a remote, uncrewed mineral-processing site at a near-Earth asteroid (NEA), 0.1–2 AU from Earth;
- a fleet of 10–18 MW-class electric-propulsion (EP) cargo tugs on multi-year low-thrust trajectories;
- a receiving node at Sun–Earth L1 (SEL1).

Before all of that, 0A must operate 4–10 rendezvous scouts and a pathfinder demonstrator.

My position, in one sentence: **Mission Operations should be run as a remote-factory operations centre with autonomy-first supervisory control, not as a flagship-science flight-control team, and its cost is a design output of the other BOM items, not a fixed overhead.**

| | 0A (committed) | 0B (gated option, sized at KDP-0B) | Phase 0 total |
|---|---|---|---|
| Duration (ops-active) | ~5.5 yr (Y1–Y6.5) | ~6.5 yr (Y6.5–Y13), resizable | ~12 yr |
| Staff, peak / steady | 125 / ~80 avg FTE | ~230 / ~180 FTE | — |
| Cost, base range | **$165–270M** | **$400–600M** | **$0.57–0.87B** |
| Point estimate | $210M | $490M | **$0.70B** |
| Pessimistic (autonomy shortfall) | $290M | $800M | ~$1.1B |
| Annual run rate | avg ~$38M/yr, peak ~$55M/yr | steady ~$70–80M/yr | — |

**Position on the round-2 figures:**

- **Claude ($0.5–1.5B):** My base sits in the lower half of this range. The upper half corresponds to an autonomy failure. That case should be carried as a named risk in bom-0-17, not in the base estimate.
- **Gemini ($525M inside a $1.1–1.5B comms+ops line):** Close to my point estimate. However, the bundling with comms must be undone, and the figure must be split into 0A and 0B.
- **GPT ($100–300M/yr, i.e. $1–3B over 10 yr):** Rejected as a base. At $300k loaded per full-time equivalent (FTE), it implies 330–1,000 FTE, which is a flagship-scale or Rio-Tinto-scale organisation for 1 kt/yr. GPT's *low* end ($100M/yr) is, however, a credible 0B outcome if site autonomy only reaches ESA level E3. I use it as my pessimistic bound.

**What the economics gate should see:** 0B operations alone cost roughly **$30k–125k per delivered tonne** (central ~$58k/t at 1.3 kt/yr). Operations is not a rounding error on the Phase 1 business case.

---

## 1. Scope and Boundaries

### 1.1 In scope (bom-0-10)

1. **Operations staff.** Flight control, flight dynamics, site/plant/robot supervision, sustaining engineering, planning and logistics, product QA, training, and ops-level mission assurance. Covers 0A and 0B.
2. **Operations facilities.** Primary Mission Operations Centre (MOC), backup MOC, operations sustainment testbed, and operations IT.
3. **Ground operations software.** Telemetry and telecommand core, fleet manager, planning and scheduling, flight dynamics tools, plant supervisory system (manufacturing execution system, MES, plus historian), digital twin, anomaly detection, archive, and product-genealogy database. Includes its build, licences, hosting and sustainment.
4. **Execution labour** for:
   - launch and early-orbit phase (LEOP) and commissioning of every Phase 0 asset;
   - debris and contamination procedures, where bom-0-15 owns the requirement, models and hardware;
   - spares and propellant logistics planning, where bom-0-14 and bom-0-16 own the hardware and propellant.
5. **Operation of the SEL1 receiving node** until handover to the Phase 1 operator.

### 1.2 Out of scope (owned elsewhere; interfaces in §5)

| Item | Owns | bom-0-10 provides |
|---|---|---|
| bom-0-9 Comms & Ground Segment | Antennas, Deep Space Network (DSN) and commercial aperture time, link encryption, Space Link Extension (SLE) delivery to the MOC | Contact requests, priorities, link-budget usage feedback |
| bom-0-11 NRE & Qualification | Flight software development, onboard autonomy development, development testbeds | Design-for-operability requirements, ops concept, ops-led verification of autonomy |
| bom-0-7 Organisation | HR, legal, finance, corporate IT, licensing counsel | Regulatory compliance reports, ops data for licence filings |
| bom-0-14 Spares | Spare hardware | Manifest planning, failure-trend data |
| bom-0-15 Debris & Contamination | ALARP requirement, models, mitigation hardware | Execution labour, monitoring, incident reports |
| bom-0-16 EP Propellant | Iodine/argon procurement and depots | Consumption forecasts, fleet refuel scheduling |
| bom-0-17 Contingency | All programme reserve | No hidden reserve is carried in bom-0-10 |

### 1.3 Disagreement on the round-2 quantity ("10 yr")

Ten years is too short if 0B is exercised:

- 0A runs to KDP-0B at about Y6.
- 0B deployment and commissioning take about 2–3 years.
- Tug transit to SEL1 takes 1–2 years.

The first delivered tonne therefore arrives at about Y10. **I price operations per year and per phase so the 0B gate can resize the tail.** The nominal plan is about 12 years: 5.5 years of 0A and 6.5 years of 0B.

---

## 2. Design Philosophy

### 2.1 Five principles

1. **Autonomy-first, ground-supervisory.**
   - One-way light time to the NEA ranges from 50 s to 17 min, and round trips run up to about 35 min.
   - Solar conjunctions impose multi-week blackouts.
   - The site must therefore run itself. The ground sets goals, tunes the process, diagnoses root causes and approves irreversible actions.
   - Robots are never directly teleoperated at the NEA.
2. **Fleet operations, not mission operations.**
   - Ten to eighteen identical tugs are operated as a fleet, with management by exception, shared procedures and one telemetry dictionary.
   - Starlink-style automation is the model, not one control team per spacecraft.
   - Target: **≤0.5 controller-FTE per tug in cruise.**
3. **Remote-factory analogue.**
   - The best terrestrial analogue is remote-operated mining, for example Rio Tinto's Perth operations centre running Pilbara mines 1,500 km away.
   - The NEA site is structured on the ISA-95 enterprise/control-system hierarchy and run like a factory with a historian, batch records and lot genealogy.
4. **Stringency follows reversibility (D-02 applied to commanding).**
   - Reversible actions, such as process setpoint changes within an envelope or robot task assignments, are routine. One authorised operator commands them, and onboard authority applies.
   - Irreversible or hazardous actions require a two-person rule, a twin-simulated preview and a hold point. Examples: tug departure burns with product, plant thermal start, HV tether energisation after a fault, excavation-regime changes affecting ejecta, end-of-life disposal.
5. **Ops cost is designed in.**
   - Most lifetime ops cost is locked in by hardware and flight-software decisions made in 0A.
   - Mission Operations therefore holds **design-for-operability (DFO) authority** at all life-cycle reviews of bom-0-1 to 0-6 and 0-13 (§5.3).

### 2.2 What I reject

- **24/7 flagship-style staffing in 0A.** Scouts in cruise do not need it. Use lights-out monitoring with on-call staff, and staff 24/7 only for critical events.
- **One operator per robot.** If pathfinder data show this is needed, that is a KDP-0B failure signal, not a staffing plan.
- **A bespoke ground system per asset class.** One ground system covers scouts, pathfinder, tugs, site and node.
- **Funding full 0B ops build-out in 0A.** Under D-01, 0A builds only what generates gate evidence: a production-architecture supervisory system exercised on the pathfinder. Scale-up waits for KDP-0B.

---

## 3. Operational Environment and Driving Requirements

### 3.1 Latency and contact environment

| Asset | Range from Earth | One-way light time | Round trip | Contact strategy (via bom-0-9) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| SEL1 receiving node | 1.5 Mkm | 5 s | 10 s | Daily 2–4 h; near-real-time possible |
| Tugs, cruise | 0.01–1.5 AU | 0.1 s–12.5 min | up to 25 min | 1–2 h/week each, plus event passes |
| Scouts, cruise | 0.05–1.5 AU | up to 12.5 min | up to 25 min | 2–3 passes/week |
| Scouts, proximity ops | 0.1–1.5 AU | up to 12.5 min | up to 25 min | Daily 6–12 h during campaigns |
| NEA site (0B) | 0.1–2.0 AU | 50 s–16.7 min | 1.7–33 min | Daily 4–8 h; continuous during commissioning |

**Conjunction.** When the Sun–Earth–probe angle is below about 3–5°, there are blackouts of roughly 2–5 weeks. For Earth-like NEA orbits the synodic period is long, often 2–10+ years, so blackouts are rare but long and must be designed for.

### 3.2 Top-level Mission Operations requirements (proposed)

| ID | Requirement | Rationale and verification |
|---|---|---|
| MO-01 | The NEA site shall survive ≥45 days without ground contact and continue production at ≥50% of nominal rate for ≥21 days unattended. | Conjunction plus a ground-outage margin. Verified on the pathfinder (scaled, ≥14-day simulated blackout) and by twin analysis. |
| MO-02 | Ground intervention rate at 0B steady state shall be ≤0.2 interventions per robot-day (target 0.05), and ≤1 per plant-day. | Main ops-cost driver. Measured on the pathfinder; this is a KDP-0B evidence item. |
| MO-03 | Tug cruise operations shall require ≤0.5 controller-FTE per tug. | Fleet automation. |
| MO-04 | Hazardous or irreversible commands shall carry two-person authorisation, a twin-predicted outcome and an onboard pre-condition check. Ground shall not attempt closed-loop control of any process with time constant <10× the round-trip light time. | Latency safety. |
| MO-05 | All assets shall enter a safe, power-positive, thermally stable state autonomously within ≤60 s of a fault. Ground shall acknowledge within one contact plus one round-trip light time. | Standard fault protection. |
| MO-06 | ≥99% of downlinked telemetry shall be captured and archived. Raw data shall be retained ≥15 years, and science/characterisation data released openly (PDS4-compatible) within 12 months unless export-controlled. | Non-profit open-data mandate. |
| MO-07 | Every shipped product lot shall be traceable to its mining cell, beneficiation batch, process batch, assay and tug manifest. | Phase 1 material/purity/date specification. |
| MO-08 | The backup MOC shall assume safety-critical positions within ≤4 h and full operations within ≤72 h. | Single-site loss. |
| MO-09 | The ground system shall meet NIST SP 800-53 moderate baseline (high for command paths), with zero-trust architecture, hardware-token two-person command signing and an air-gapped command-authorisation enclave. | Uncrewed high-value assets. |
| MO-10 | Ops cost shall be reported as $/delivered-tonne and FTE/asset every quarter, with a not-to-exceed tripwire at the 0B gate. | Economics gate (D-02). |
| MO-11 | Execution of the bom-0-15 ALARP regime: excavation and handling ejecta shall be kept below the local escape speed (computed per target) or contained, with lidar/camera monitoring and incident reporting within 24 h. | Debris/contamination requirement. |

**Physical note on MO-11.** For a 500 m NEA with bulk density 2 g/cm³, mass M ≈ 1.3×10¹¹ kg and escape speed v_esc ≈ √(2GM/r) ≈ **0.26 m/s**. For a 150 m body it is about 0.08 m/s. Excavation tooling speeds of order 0.1 m/s can therefore loft material off the body, so containment, not just procedure, is required. Ops enforces the regime; bom-0-2 and bom-0-15 own the hardware.

---

## 4. System Architecture

### 4.1 End-to-end operations architecture

```
 SPACE SEGMENT (autonomy owned by bom-0-11 SW, hardware by 0-1..0-6, 0-13)
 ┌──────────────────────────── NEA SITE (0B) ─────────────────────────────┐
```

### 4.2 Control hierarchy and autonomy tiers

Autonomy tiers are mapped to ESA ECSS-E-ST-70-11C autonomy levels (E1–E4) and to ISA-95 levels.

```
 Tier  Where        Time scale     Function                          ECSS / ISA-95
 ────  ───────────  ─────────────  ────────────────────────────────  ─────────────
 T0    each asset   ms – s         reflexes, FDIR, safe mode         E3 / L1
 T1    each asset   min – h        task execution (excavate cell,    E3–E4 / L2
                                   thrust arc, transfer product)
 T2    SAC @ NEA    h – days       site scheduling, power arbitration E4 / L2–L3
                                   across robots/plant/storage,
                                   batch sequencing, local recovery
 T3    Ground MOC   days – weeks   campaign goals, process tuning,   — / L3
                                   root cause, fleet logistics,
                                   irreversible-action approval
 T4    Programme    months         gates, Phase 1 demand, target     — / L4
                                   changes
```

**Required autonomy levels.**

| Level | Assets |
|---|---|
| **E4** (goal-based onboard re-planning) | NEA site (SAC), tugs in cruise |
| **E3** (event-based onboard operations) | Scouts, robots individually, SEL1 node |
| E2 (time-tagged commands) | Not used for any Phase 0 asset |

**Commanding granularity.**

- Ground uplinks weekly campaign plans, for example: "process 18 t ore this week, prioritise zone C, hold furnace below X kW during storage-recharge windows".
- Daily delta plans adjust the campaign.
- Robots receive task-level goals from the SAC, never motion commands from Earth.
- At SEL1 (10 s round trip), supervised near-real-time manipulation is allowed for product acceptance and docking contingencies.

**Bridging latency.** The ground digital twin runs **predictive displays**. Operators see the twin's estimate of "now" at the site, with uncertainty bounds, propagated from the last telemetry plus the commanded plan. Divergence between twin and telemetry is itself an anomaly trigger.

### 4.3 Operations concepts by phase

**0A: scouts.**

- **Cruise:** Autonomous EP thrust arcs. Weekly orbit determination (OD), with trajectory updates every 2–4 weeks. Monitoring is lights-out.
- **Approach:** Optical navigation campaign over 30–60 days.
- **Proximity operations:** 3–6 month characterisation campaigns. Small-body gravity and shape modelling follow the OSIRIS-REx and Hayabusa2 heritage, with more onboard autonomy.
- **Data products:** Feed the **target gate** (D-02 discriminating gate).

**0A: pathfinder (bom-0-12).** This is the ops-critical demonstrator. It must run the **same SAC software architecture and ground system** intended for 0B, so that KDP-0B evidence is about the flight-like system and not a surrogate. Required ops evidence for KDP-0B:

1. ≥60 days continuous autonomous operation, including ≥1 commanded 14-day zero-contact interval.
2. Intervention rate measured and trending to ≤0.5 per asset-day, with an extrapolation case to MO-02.
3. Zero unrecoverable operator-induced anomalies.
4. Twin prediction error within an agreed envelope for key process variables (furnace/reduction temperature, throughput, product composition).
5. At least one end-to-end lot genealogy record from mining cell to assay.

**0B: deployment and commissioning (~18–24 months).**

- Covers LEOP for each tug and cargo element, site build-up and power-on, robot deployment, and progressive plant start-up.
- This is the staffing surge: 24/7 operations, continuous site contact through bom-0-9, and daily anomaly boards.

**0B: production (steady state).**

- The site runs at E4.
- Ground staffing is 24/7 with 3 core positions overnight and 8–10 daytime positions.
- Tugs cycle the NEA → SEL1 route, with departure burns as irreversible-action hold points.
- Product lots are certified against the Phase 1 specification before tug acceptance and again at SEL1 receipt.

**Wind-down or Earth-fallback.** If microgravity metallurgy fails at KDP-0B, or during 0B, ops scales down to scouts, pathfinder disposal and tug repurposing. The trained team is the asset most easily redirected to Earth-supplied-material logistics. This is part of the real-option value of D-01.

---

## 5. Subsystems and Interfaces

### 5.1 Ground software (functional specification)

| Element | Baseline approach | Scale (0B) | TRL now |
|---|---|---|---|
| Front end / SLE gateway | COTS or open-source CCSDS SLE (RAF/RCF/CLTU) | ~25 simultaneous assets | 9 |
| TM/TC core | Open-source (Yamcs / OpenC3 COSMOS), XTCE dictionaries | 50k–150k site parameters; ~5k per tug | 9 |
| Command Authorisation Enclave | Custom on hardened COTS, HSM tokens | 2-person rule, signed command loads | 7 |
| Fleet manager | Custom on TM/TC core; rules plus ML triage | 10–18 tugs, 4–10 scouts | 6–7 |
| Planning and scheduling | Goal/timeline planner (ASPEN/CASPER-class concepts); contact scheduling interface to bom-0-9 | Weekly campaigns, daily deltas | 6 |
| Flight dynamics | GMAT (open source) plus low-thrust optimiser; OD with optical navigation; JPL MONTE optional via licence | 25+ trajectories; NEA gravity field | 8 (prox ops) / 7 (fleet automation) |
| Plant supervisory / MES / historian | ISA-95 L3 MES and time-series historian (PI-class or open-source) | ~10⁵ tags at 0.1–1 Hz after downsampling | 9 on Earth / 4 for remote space plant |
| Digital twin | Process simulation (reduction, magnetic separation, melt/consolidation), regolith-tool interaction, power/thermal | Faster than real time ×10 | 2–3 for microgravity metallurgy |
| Anomaly detection | Residual-to-twin plus per-parameter learned baselines | All assets | 5–6 |
| Product genealogy / QA DB | Relational DB, immutable lot records | ~10³–10⁴ lots/yr | 8 |
| Archive | Object storage, PDS4 export | 0.1–0.6 PB total | 9 |

**Data volume basis.** The round-2 figure of 2.5 TB/day is rejected, consistent with bom-0-9.

| Source | Rate during contact | Contact | Daily volume |
|---|---|---|---|
| NEA site | 2–10 Mbps | 4–8 h/day | ~4–36 GB/day |
| Tug fleet (18 tugs) | — | weekly | <1 GB/day total |
| Scouts in proximity ops | — | daily | 1–5 GB/day |
| **Total** | | | **~10–50 GB/day** |

Over 12 years this gives about 50–200 TB raw, or ≤0.6 PB with derived products. **Storage and compute are not cost drivers**: about $0.2–0.5M/yr hosted.

### 5.2 Facilities specification

| Facility | Specification | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| **Primary MOC** | 1,800–2,500 m² leased and fitted out. Operations floor ~400 m² with 24–32 consoles, plus a 6-console critical-events room. Simulation/training room ~150 m². Anomaly room. ~150 on-site seats; the rest hybrid. | 0B peak ~230 FTE; about 60–70% on-site |

### 5.3 Design-for-operability requirements flowed to other items

8. **Ops participation as a voting member** at every PDR/CDR/ORR for bom-0-1 through 0-6, 0-12 and 0-13.

## 9. "Manufacturing" Considerations for an Operations Line

Operations does not build flight hardware. It does have production-like activities:

1. **Ground system production.**

   - Use a DevSecOps pipeline with signed builds and a testbed gate before any operational deployment.
2. **Procedure production.**
   - Procedures are written as executable scripts (COSMOS/Yamcs scripting) with formal pre- and post-conditions, not as documents.
   - Each tug procedure is written once and is fleet-wide.
   - Estimated library: ~800–1,500 procedures in 0B.
3. **Product as manufactured output.**
   - The NEA site is a factory. Ops runs ISA-88 batch records and ISA-95 MES functions.
   - The QA team issues **lot certificates** against the Phase 1 material/purity/date specification: Fe-Ni composition, impurity limits (S, P, C, O), form factor and mass.
   - Each certificate cross-checks SAC assay telemetry against a sampled re-assay at SEL1 (bom-0-13 instrument).
4. **Configuration control.**
   - Ops maintains the as-flown configuration database for every asset: software versions, parameter tables and hardware states.

## 1. Recommended Approach and Design Philosophy

The Phase 0 mission architecture—mining and processing Fe-Ni at a Near-Earth Asteroid (NEA) and transporting it via 10–18 MW-class electric propulsion tugs—presents a unique operational challenge. The light-time delay to a typical NEA (ranging from 1 to 15+ minutes one-way) strictly precludes "joystick" teleoperation. 

Our core philosophy is **Supervisory Control and Management by Exception**. The Mission Operations Center (MOC) will not fly the spacecraft; it will manage the fleet. 
*   **Phase 0A (Pathfinders & Scouts):** High-touch operations. Human operators validate autonomous sequences, build the operational knowledge base, and train the ground-based AI fault-detection models.
*   **Phase 0B (Industrial Production):** Low-touch, high-volume logistics. Operations shift to a "factory floor" mentality, utilizing highly automated scheduling, Digital Twin telemetry monitoring, and automated trajectory optimization for the cargo tug fleet.

**Disagreement with Round-2 Figures:**

### 2.1 Subsystems Breakdown
1.  **Flight Dynamics Facility (FDF):** Manages continuous low-thrust trajectory optimization for the 10–18 MW-class cargo tugs. Calculates burn schedules for iodine/argon EP systems and manages SEL1 rendezvous phasing.
2.  **Payload & Mine Operations (PMO):** Monitors the 1-3 kV tethered mining robots and the primary processing plant at the NEA. Focuses on throughput metrics, thermal rejection (radiator health), and tool-wear prediction.
3.  **Fleet Logistics & Scheduling:** A supply-chain management system adapted for orbital mechanics. Tracks ore inventory at the NEA, tug transit states, and SEL1 delivery schedules.
4.  **Digital Twin & Anomaly Resolution:** Ingests telemetry to maintain a real-time physical model of all assets. Used to simulate fault recovery commands before transmission.

## 3. Autonomy, Control, and Communication Requirements

*   **Light-Time Delay Handling:** All mining robots and processing plants must possess local Level 4 autonomy (capable of safe-mode, thermal management, and basic obstacle avoidance without Earth intervention).
*   **Command Uplink:** Ground ops will uplink macro-commands (e.g., "Excavate Sector 4 for 12 hours", "Initiate return transit to SEL1"). 
*   **Telemetry Downlink:** To respect the bandwidth limits of the comms architecture, routine telemetry is processed at the NEA edge. Only aggregated health states, production metrics, and high-res anomaly data (triggered by local fault detection) are downlinked.
*   **Cybersecurity:** End-to-end AES-256 encryption. The MOC operates on a physically air-gapped network for command generation, utilizing a strict zero-trust architecture.

## 6. Risk Assessment

1.  **Operator Fatigue in Low-Touch Ops (Risk: High):** Highly automated systems can lead to operator complacency. 
    *   *Mitigation:* Implement active-engagement training, regular simulation of critical anomalies ("fire drills"), and rotate staff between planning and monitoring.
2.  **Software Development Overrun (Risk: Medium):** Building a bespoke multi-agent Digital Twin for space mining is unprecedented.
    *   *Mitigation:* Leverage existing open-source and commercial satellite fleet management software (e.g., Major Tom, Yamcs) as the base layer; only build custom modules for the mining/processing payloads.
3.  **Loss of Command Link during Critical Operations (Risk: Low/Catastrophic):** 
    *   *Mitigation:* Strict requirement that no action requiring sub-minute latency is ever initiated without local autonomous safing capability. Battery backups on tethered robots (10-50 kWh) ensure safe shutdown if site power or comms fail.

### 1.2 Scope boundaries

| Included in bom-0-10 | Explicitly owned elsewhere |
|---|---|
| Flight controllers, mission planners, flight dynamics, operations safety, and mission-level anomaly management | Programme executives, corporate administration, legal and institutional governance: bom-0-7 |
| Mission-control room fit-out, consoles, operational computing, and operational software | Antennas, RF terminals, communications relays, carrier connectivity and network-service purchases: bom-0-9 |

| Operational use of simulators, rehearsals, controller certification, and procedure validation | Pathfinder spacecraft and flight experiments: bom-0-12 |

## 2. Recommended design philosophy

### 2.1 Operate an industrial system, not a collection of science spacecraft

A scout campaign can tolerate individually crafted command sequences. An industrial fleet cannot.

By 0B, the system must support:

- Repeated production and shipment cycles.
- Fleet-wide configuration control.
- Material pedigree and custody.
- Predictive maintenance.
- Scheduling constrained by power, heat rejection, storage, vehicle availability, trajectories, and receiving-node capacity.
- Safe suspension of production without continuous Earth supervision.

The central operational object should be a **validated work package**:

> Acquire feedstock → process batch → characterize product → certify lot → load cargo → transfer custody → transport → receive and accept.

Each package carries resource limits, prerequisites, abort conditions, and evidence requirements.

### 2.2 Separate safety authority from production optimization

A production scheduler must never be able to override:

- Electrical protection.
- Thermal limits.
- Excavation or anchoring stability limits.
- Containment limits.
- Vehicle separation constraints.
- Docking interlocks.
- Propulsion inhibit regions.
- Receiving-node acceptance restrictions.

These constraints belong in independently verified protection functions aboard the relevant asset. Ground operations can change authorized operating envelopes only through controlled procedures.

### 2.3 Preserve optionality through 0A

Do not build a fully staffed industrial control centre before target, demand, economics, and licence gates close.

Use modular software and leased facilities in 0A. Expand staffing, availability, simulator capacity, and fleet scheduling after authorization.

Earth-supplied material remains the programme fallback if microgravity metallurgy fails. Operations should therefore support receiving-node logistics independently of whether the accepted cargo originated at the NEA or Earth.

## 3. System architecture

```text
                  PROGRAMME / PHASE 1 GOVERNANCE
              demand, licence conditions, acceptance criteria
                                  |
                                  v
                  MISSION OPERATIONS AUTHORITY
             flight rules / configuration / release approval
                                  |
           +----------------------+----------------------+
           |                      |                      |
           v                      v                      v
   Mission planning       Flight dynamics       Product logistics
   and fleet schedule     and navigation        and custody records
           |                      |                      |
           +----------------------+----------------------+
                                  |
                     Command validation gateway
                    independent safety-rule checks
                                  |
                Communications service — bom-0-9
                                  |
             +--------------------+--------------------+
             |                    |                    |
             v                    v                    v
      Scout/pathfinder       NEA site control      Tug fleet
      local autonomy         power/mining/plant    local autonomy
                                  |                    |
                                  +----------+---------+
                                             |
                                             v
                                  SEL1 receiving operations
                                  reference case: bom-0-13
```

The receiving node’s hardware and embedded controls belong to bom-0-13. Its mission-level scheduling and custody coordination are performed through this operations system.

### 3.1 Operational authority

- **Mission director:** authorizes operational campaigns and significant risk acceptance within approved programme authority.
- **Flight director:** controls execution and anomaly response.
- **Vehicle/site authority:** owns the approved operating envelope for each asset.
- **Independent safety officer:** can stop hazardous operations; cannot be overruled by production scheduling.
- **Product acceptance authority:** accepts or rejects delivered lots against the signed Phase 1 specification.
- **Configuration control board:** approves changes to software, procedures, command dictionaries, and flight rules.

The person who prepares a hazardous command must not be its sole approver.

---

## 4. Technical specifications

These are proposed operations-system requirements, not claimed characteristics of existing hardware.

### 4.1 Capacity and performance

| Attribute | 0A requirement | 0B requirement |
|---|---:|---:|
| Independently addressed flight/site entities | 16 minimum | 64 minimum |
| Detailed subsystem endpoints | 250 | 2,000 |
| Concurrent high-attention campaigns | 2 | 4 |
| Permanently staffed console positions | 3–5 during active flight operations | 12–18 |
| Command/activity time resolution | 1 s for mission scheduling; finer control local | Same |
| Operational telemetry retained online | 180 days minimum | 365 days minimum |
| Engineering/product records | Programme life plus contractual retention period | Same |
| Ground command-service availability | 99.5% monthly | 99.9% monthly |
| Primary control-centre recovery | Within 8 h | Within 2 h |
| Planned unattended safe interval | Asset-specific; demonstrated in 0A | At least 30 days as a design objective |
| Minimum disconnected safe-survival demonstration | 72 h, progressing to campaign-specific cases | Required for applicable operating modes |

**Availability excludes external communications coverage.** Ground-system availability, link availability, and spacecraft availability must be reported separately.

The 30-day objective is not permission to run an unvalidated production process unattended for a month. During an extended outage, a plant may suspend production and enter a contained thermal/electrical safe state.

### 4.2 Ground facilities

Use one primary operations centre and one geographically separated recovery centre.

| Parameter | 0A | 0B |
|---|---:|---:|
| Primary operations floor and support space | 400–700 m² | 800–1,400 m² |
| Recovery-site dedicated space | 100–200 m² | 200–400 m² |
| Primary installed console positions | 10–16 | 24–36 |
| Recovery-site console positions | 4–6 | 8–12 |
| Primary operational IT racks | 4–8 | 10–20 |
| Average IT electrical load | 20–50 kW | 60–150 kW |
| Facility electrical demand, including cooling | 35–100 kW | 100–300 kW |
| Protected operational storage | 0.5–1 PB usable | 2–5 PB usable |

Storage figures include replicas, simulation outputs, software artefacts, and engineering records—not a corresponding continuous space-to-Earth data requirement.

Ground equipment mass is not a mission-driving metric. No dedicated flight hardware mass is allocated to this item. Flight computing, sensors, and communications equipment remain in their vehicle or site BOMs.

### 4.3 Resilience

- Independent power feeds where practical.
- UPS sized for orderly transfer and shutdown; generator-backed critical loads.
- Geographically separate backups and immutable configuration archives.
- Independent command-release credentials at the recovery site.
- Quarterly recovery exercises.
- Annual full operational transfer to the recovery site.
- No requirement for the backup site to duplicate every engineering workstation or simulator.

---

## 5. Subsystems and interfaces

### 5.1 Mission planning and fleet scheduler

The scheduler shall combine:

- Trajectory windows and navigation uncertainty.
- Available tug and payload capacity.
- EP power and propellant budgets.
- Site power allocation and storage state.
- Processing and radiator constraints.
- Robot maintenance and battery availability.
- Docking/loading opportunities.
- Product acceptance and storage capacity.
- Communications coverage.

Use a **rolling 90-day strategic plan**, a **14-day executable planning horizon**, and a **24–72-hour committed activity window**, adjusted by mission phase.

The optimizer proposes plans; an independently implemented validator checks hard constraints before release.

### 5.2 Flight dynamics and navigation

Provide:

- Orbit determination and covariance propagation.
- Low-thrust trajectory reconstruction and replanning.
- Optical navigation support.
- Target-body rotation and shape-model updates.
- Proximity-operation corridor design.
- Conjunction screening and uncertainty-aware maneuver assessment.
- SEL1 arrival/departure planning appropriate to the selected receiving-node orbit.

During commissioning and encounter phases, navigation support is continuously available. During routine cruise, processing can be batched.

No vehicle enters proximity operations solely because its nominal trajectory is clear; uncertainty bounds and failed-thrust cases must also satisfy the approved corridor.

### 5.3 Telemetry, command, and event processing

Use CCSDS-compatible external interfaces where applicable, with versioned internal schemas.

Required functions:

- Time-tagged telemetry and data-quality flags.
- Limit checking that accounts for operating mode.
- Event correlation across assets.
- Command authentication, authorization, expiration, and replay protection.
- Positive acknowledgement and execution-state reconciliation.
- Complete command provenance.

At the application layer, commands require identifiers and reconciliation logic so that retransmission cannot inadvertently repeat an irreversible action.

### 5.4 Engineering state model

Maintain an operational state estimator covering:

- Power and energy.
- Thermal state.
- Propellant and consumables.
- Wear and remaining useful life.
- Material inventories.
- Product lots and custody.
- Navigation state and uncertainty.

Avoid treating a “digital twin” as a certification substitute. Every prediction must carry model version, calibration status, and uncertainty. Safety decisions cannot depend on an unvalidated model merely because its visualization looks convincing.

### 5.5 Product traceability

For every delivered Fe-Ni lot, retain:

- Source location and feedstock campaign.
- Processing recipe and equipment configuration.
- Mass estimate and uncertainty.
- Composition and impurity measurements.
- Applicable mechanical or fabrication qualification evidence.
- Sampling and calibration records.
- Container identity and transfer history.
- Receiving inspection and acceptance decision.

Phase 1 must specify **composition, allowable contaminants, physical form, quantity, delivery date, and acceptance method** before 0B commitment. Operations cannot compensate for an undefined product.

---

## 6. Autonomy, control, and communications

### 6.1 Four levels of control

| Level | Responsibility | Typical timescale |
|---|---|---|
| Protection | Trips, isolation, thermal/electrical protection, collision inhibition | Milliseconds–seconds |
| Local control | Process regulation, robotics, navigation and stationkeeping | Subseconds–minutes |
| Supervisory autonomy | Task execution, bounded recovery, resource arbitration | Minutes–days |
| Earth mission control | Campaign priorities, operating envelopes, configuration changes | Hours–months |

Ground control is deliberately outside fast control loops.

### 6.2 Communications planning basis

A fixed daily volume is inappropriate until target geometry and instrument duty cycles are known. For preliminary allocation:

| Traffic | 0A | 0B |
|---|---:|---:|
| Routine compressed engineering and selected science/inspection data | 1–10 GB/day | 5–30 GB/day aggregate |
| Campaign burst | 20–100 GB/event | 50–250 GB/event |
| Command/planning uplink | Generally <100 MB/day | Generally <1 GB/day |

The 0B routine range corresponds to approximately **0.46–2.8 Mbps averaged over a day**, before link overhead. Scheduled contact rates must be higher when contact duty cycle is low.

These are **operations allocation assumptions**, not a link-budget result. High-resolution inspection imagery should be selectively downlinked; continuous raw robot video is not the baseline.

Commands and health summaries receive priority over bulk imagery. Store-and-forward operation and resumable transfers are mandatory.

### 6.3 Delay and outage tolerance

Actual delay follows the selected trajectory and target. Software should support:

- One-way light time from seconds to approximately 30 minutes.
- Irregular contact schedules.
- Several-day planned outages.
- Longer solar-conjunction interruptions, evaluated using the chosen geometry.
- No remote joystick dependency for industrial operations.

The safety case must explicitly define the state of each subsystem during loss of communications: continue, finish current task, suspend, or isolate.

### 6.4 Cybersecurity

- Hardware-backed command-signing keys.
- Segregated development, simulation, operations, and business networks.
- Two-person approval for hazardous commands and trust-store changes.
- Signed software loads and controlled rollback.
- Independent security monitoring.
- No uncontrolled direct vendor access to flight-command systems.
- Tested response to compromised ground credentials.

---

## 7. Staffing and operational model

### 7.1 Recommended workforce

Figures are average paid FTE during each phase, including shift relief and directly assigned operational engineering.

| Function | 0A FTE | 0B FTE |
|---|---:|---:|
| Flight directors, controllers, and shift coordination | 16–24 | 45–65 |
| Flight dynamics, navigation, and trajectory planning | 10–16 | 30–44 |
| Site/process/robotics operations engineering | 14–22 | 25–36 |
| Software, data systems, and operational IT | 12–18 | 28–40 |
| Mission planning and logistics | 10–14 | 18–26 |
| Safety, cybersecurity, configuration and quality | 8–12 | 16–24 |
| Training, simulation, and operational integration | 10–14 | 18–25 |
| **Total** | **80–120** | **180–260** |

These are not all console operators.

A continuously occupied console typically requires approximately **5–5.5 paid FTE**, allowing for leave, training, sickness, and handover. Thus, 12–18 continuously staffed 0B positions consume roughly 60–99 FTE before specialist day staff and engineering support.

### 7.2 Operating pattern

**0A**

- Day-shift engineering and planning.
- Continuous coverage during active commissioning, encounters, hazardous tests, and major anomalies.
- Reduced staffed coverage plus on-call response during demonstrated low-risk cruise, where allowed by flight rules.

**0B**

- Continuous fleet-level supervision.
- Specialists on day shift and on call.
- Dedicated commissioning teams temporarily formed for new assets.
- No permanent one-controller-per-robot model.

Success is measured partly by reducing operator interventions per production campaign without hiding unresolved anomalies.

---

## 8. Manufacturing, procurement, and maintainability

This item is dominated by software integration and service delivery rather than aerospace manufacturing.

Recommended procurement:

1. **Lease ordinary office and control-room space.**
2. Use commercial server, storage, and workstation hardware.
3. Procure an established telemetry/command core rather than developing one from scratch.
4. Own the mission data model, operational procedures, interfaces, and configuration repository.
5. Require exportable archives and documented APIs to prevent vendor lock-in.
6. Maintain reproducible software builds and a software bill of materials.
7. Qualify representative ground hardware configurations rather than freezing obsolete server models for ten years.

For ground hardware, plan rolling refreshes on roughly four-to-five-year intervals. Operational software should use controlled releases with regression testing; an urgent security patch still requires a defined emergency release process.

Flight software production and qualified onboard computing remain outside this item.

---

## 9. Development roadmap and readiness

NASA-style lifecycle gates govern the programme, with TRL and AD² assessments for critical technology. Operational readiness reviews complement—not replace—technology qualification.

### Stage 1: Architecture and requirements — 0A year 1

Deliver:

- Operations concept.
- Authority matrix.
- Interface control documents.
- Preliminary staffing and communications demand.
- Hazardous-command policy.
- Initial integrated simulation environment.
- Initial contingency procedures.

### Stage 2: Scout operations and ground integration — 0A years 1–2

Demonstrate:

- Multi-asset planning.
- Independent command validation.
- Navigation and delayed communications.
- Configuration-controlled procedures.
- Backup-centre recovery.

Internal critical functions should achieve TRL 4–5 evidence where applicable.

### Stage 3: Pathfinder industrial campaign — 0A years 2–4

Demonstrate the end-to-end operational chain:

1. Plan and authorize a bounded processing campaign.
2. Execute with delayed or interrupted communications.
3. Recover from selected equipment faults.
4. Maintain material records.
5. Produce an auditable acceptance package.
6. Suspend safely and restart under controlled authority.

### Stage 4: KDP-0B evidence package

KDP-0B requires:

- Target gate passed.
- Signed demand with product specification and dates.
- Economics case including operations cost and fallback comparison.
- Applicable licence and operating conditions.
- Every project-ending technology at **TRL 6 in a relevant environment, without waivers**.
- Critical integrated operational chains demonstrated in relevant conditions.
- Closed high-consequence operational hazards.
- Staffing, training, and purchased communications plans consistent with the selected architecture.

A ground simulation alone cannot establish relevant-environment maturity for a project-ending microgravity processing or autonomous site-control technology.

### Stage 5: Incremental industrial activation

Commission production in bounded increments:

- Site utilities.
- Single mining/processing chain.
- First accepted product lot.
- First cargo transfer.
- First receiving-node acceptance.
- Sustained multi-asset campaigns.

Do not activate the entire fleet and full processing throughput simultaneously.

---

## 10. Cost estimate

### 10.1 Lifecycle estimate

**Constant FY2026 USD, millions; excludes bom-0-17 reserve.**

| Cost element | 0A: 4 years | 0B: 6 years | Basis |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Direct operations workforce | 77–154 | 281–530 | FTE above; $240–320k/FTE-year in 0A, $260–340k in 0B |
| External software products and integration | 65–110 | 90–170 | Vendor work, licences, support, specialist integration; excludes work already in staff costs |
| Operations facilities and computing capital | 15–30 | 20–40 | Fit-out, servers, backup site, refresh |
| Recurring facilities and operational services | 15–25 | 45–80 | Lease, utilities, hosting and non-telecom support |
| External rehearsal, training and independent operational assurance | 15–25 | 25–45 | Purchased exercises and independent review; internal labour counted above |
| **Total** | **187–344** | **461–865** | |
| **Combined conditional lifecycle** | | **648–1,209** | **Approximately $0.65–1.21B** |

Loaded labour includes compensation, benefits, contractor fee where applicable, and directly attributable employment overhead. Programme-level corporate infrastructure is not added again here.

This is a planning estimate, not a probabilistic confidence interval. Dominant uncertainty lies in autonomy maturity, target accessibility, commissioning duration, and whether the fleet can share operators.

### 10.2 Incremental annual cost

- **Extended 0A, flight assets active:** approximately **$35–65M/year**, depending on campaign intensity.
- **Mature 0B recurring operations:** approximately **$75–130M/year**.
- **Heavy commissioning/anomaly year:** approximately **$100–160M/year**.
- **New simultaneous production site:** requires separate estimation; it is not covered by the base range.

Software development and capital expenditure make early years uneven; lifecycle totals should not be divided into identical annual appropriations.

### 10.3 Position on round-2 estimates

- **Claude: $0.5–1.5B total.** Broadly credible. My lower bound is higher because I explicitly include recovery capability, industrial process specialists, navigation, cybersecurity, and sustained operational assurance.
- **Gemini: $525M.** Too low for my recommended ten-year baseline unless autonomy performs unusually well, staffing remains lean, or substantial software and operations costs reside elsewhere. It is a possible stretch case, not a sound central allocation.
- **GPT: $100–300M/year.** The lower portion is plausible for industrial commissioning and difficult operations. Sustained $300M/year is not justified for one site and 10–18 tugs without major additional scope or persistent operational failures.

At 1 kt/year, mature operations alone contribute roughly **$75–130/kg delivered**. Across 0.6–2.5 kt/year, the corresponding range is approximately **$30–217/kg**. This excludes development, hardware, launch, communications, propellant, and replacements. Phase 0 remains a capability programme, not an asserted cost-saving scheme.

---

## 11. Principal risks and mitigations

| Risk | Consequence | Required mitigation |
|---|---|---|
| Autonomy fails to reduce interventions | Staffing growth; throughput shortfall | Pathfinder measurements of intervention frequency and recovery success |
| Common-mode fleet software defect | Multiple simultaneous losses | Staggered deployment, canary asset, rollback and heterogeneous protection paths |
| Long communications outage | Equipment damage or unsafe production | Validated disconnected states and resource-reserve rules |
| Navigation uncertainty near small body | Collision, plume disturbance, loss of asset | Covariance-aware corridors and local sensing |
| Production optimization defeats safety margins | Thermal, electrical or containment event | Independent interlocks and command validator |
| Product records diverge from physical cargo | Rejection or unusable deliveries | Container identity, mass reconciliation and custody checks |
| Ground credential compromise | Unauthorized commands | Segregation, signing, dual approval and tested key revocation |
| Simultaneous commissioning exceeds staff capacity | Error and delayed response | Cap concurrent high-attention campaigns |
| Licensing conditions restrict operations | Lower throughput or redesign | Licence gate before irreversible industrial commitment |
| Plant never achieves usable metallurgy | No industrial product | Preserve Earth-supply fallback and terminate or redirect 0B |

### Debris and contamination control

Under interim D-03, operations shall implement ALARP and the eventual approved design ceiling. **This proposal does not invent a release percentage.**

Operational rules must address:

- Particle size and velocity distributions, not just total mass.
- Release direction and trajectory evolution.
- Dust charging and redistribution.
- Plume/particle interactions.
- Sensor detection limits.
- Stop-work criteria.
- Containment verification after a fault.

The numerical ceiling and compliance method belong to the modelling, test, and licensing process led under bom-0-15. The operations system must be able to enforce whichever limits are approved.

---

## 12. Open engineering decisions

1. **Target geometry:** rotation, communications visibility, local gravity, regolith behaviour, and solar environment determine staffing and autonomy requirements.
2. **Permitted unattended states:** which mining, processing, and loading tasks may continue during extended loss of contact?
3. **Phase 1 product specification:** acceptable Fe-Ni chemistry, physical form, characterization method, and delivery timing remain decisive.
4. **Fleet utilization:** tug count does not establish annual delivery; round-trip duration, maintenance and loading availability must close the manifest.
5. **Receiving-node operations:** docking, storage, inspection and rejected-lot handling must be agreed with Phase 1.
6. **Control partitioning:** which functions are owned by robot, plant, site, and fleet controllers?
7. **Propellant-specific hazards:** iodine and argon impose different handling, contamination and operational constraints.
8. **Safe-state energy:** storage and thermal design must support the agreed disconnected survival case.
9. **Operational economics:** what measured intervention rate is affordable at contracted throughput?
10. **Shutdown and disposal:** approved end-of-life states are required for every asset before launch.

## Final recommendation

Authorize **a $187–344M mission-operations provision for 0A**, with spending released by lifecycle milestones. Carry **$461–865M for six years of 0B** only as a conditional planning allowance.

The most important 0A result is not a polished control room. It is evidence that an integrated, delayed-communications industrial system can **produce a traceable acceptable lot, survive faults, and reach a safe state without continuous human intervention**. Without that evidence—and the target, demand, economics and licence gates—industrial operations should not be funded.
